summary: Defines the policy for using 233/8 for statically assigned multicast addresses. It is a Best Current Practice.

plainLanguage.summary: GLOP addressing gives each eligible Autonomous System a fixed block of multicast addresses within 233/8. The block is formed from the AS number, but the method only fits two-octet AS numbers.

subtitle: Divides the 233/8 multicast block into fixed allocations based on two-octet AS numbers.

tldr.problem: Some multicast applications need group addresses that remain fixed, but dynamic allocation does not meet every deployment's needs and there was no broadly agreed allocation scheme.
tldr.mechanism: The first octet is 233, the next 16 bits hold an assigned Autonomous System number, and the remaining 8 bits are local, providing one /24 per AS.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an automatic allocation scheme for two-octet AS numbers and obsoletes RFC 2770. It does not work with extended AS numbers.

today: RFC 3180 is a Best Current Practice and obsoletes RFC 2770. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why Fixed Multicast Addresses
sections.content:
Multicast addresses were often allocated dynamically, but some applications need addresses that stay fixed for longer periods. The memo gives content aggregators as an example and notes that the community lacked a coherent allocation scheme.

This approach addresses a subset of multicast allocation needs, specifically cases not covered by Source Specific Multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Some applications need multicast addresses that stay the same rather than being assigned dynamically. This memo defines one way to allocate fixed addresses.

sections.title: How the 233/8 Block Is Divided
sections.content:
The high-order octet is 233, the next 16 bits contain an already assigned Autonomous System (AS) number, and the last 8 bits are for local use. This gives each AS one /24 block.

For example, the RFC shows AS 5662 mapping to 233.22.30/24. Using the assigned AS number means the allocation is automatic and requires no additional registration step.
sections.plainLanguage: The address includes a network's AS number, followed by bits it can use locally. This lets the network determine its own block without a separate registration.

sections.title: The Two-Octet AS Limit
sections.content: The scheme works only with two-octet AS numbers. It cannot represent an AS number extension because the address has only 16 bits available for the AS number.
sections.plainLanguage: The address leaves 16 bits for the AS number. A longer AS number does not fit in this format.

sections.title: Security and Allocation Notes
sections.content:
The memo says this approach may reduce exposure to denial-of-service attacks based on dynamic allocation. Because dynamic assignment does not cross domain boundaries in this scheme, familiar within-domain security techniques can be used.

IANA assigned 233/8 for this purpose. RFC 3180 obsoletes RFC 2770.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo notes that fixed allocation may reduce some risks tied to dynamic assignment. It also records the block's assignment and replaces the earlier RFC 2770 description.
